I work hard at keeping busy with other things
repeatedly blame myself for what happened

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt

vignette:
Maria Garcia was seventy-eight years old when she finally agreed to see a therapist, though she had been carrying the weight of a single night for more than forty years. She remembered the diesel fumes first—the sharp, oily smell that had clung to her clothes as she and her husband huddled in the back of a pickup truck, their two young children pressed between strangers, crossing the border at dusk. The truck had broken down twice, and each time the men had whispered urgently in the dark while Maria sat frozen, her arms wrapped around her daughter and son, her eyes fixed on the muddy ground where rotting leaves and spilled gasoline mixed into a thick, acrid odor she could still summon at will. She had not spoken of that night in decades, and when she tried to put it into words for the intake clinician, her throat closed and her hands began to tremble. The story existed only in fragments—a flash of headlights, the feel of gravel under her palms, the sound of her own breathing—but never as a coherent narrative she could tell aloud. What came out instead was a single, repeated question: why had this happened to her? She had been a schoolteacher in her home country, a woman who believed in order and fairness, and the random brutality of that journey—the soldiers at the checkpoint, the family that had been pulled from a truck ahead of theirs—made no sense. She had gone over it so often in her mind that the details had worn smooth, like stones in a river, but the guilt never faded. She blamed herself for not having planned better, for not having hidden more money, for the moment her son had cried and she had clamped her hand over his mouth until he was silent. That guilt was the sharpest thing she carried.

In the years since, Maria had built a quiet life. She worked as a librarian at a public branch in a small Midwestern town, a job she had taken after retiring from teaching, because the library felt safe. She spent her days shelving books, cataloging donations, and keeping herself busy at all costs. The moment a lull came, her mind would drift back to the truck, to the smell of diesel and wet earth, and so she filled every minute with tasks. She volunteered for extra shifts, organized the children’s reading hour, and offered to re-label the entire reference section. Her colleagues praised her dedication, but Maria knew it was a wall she had built. She had become hypervigilant in ways that wore her out—she scanned the faces of every patron who walked through the doors, listened for raised voices, and positioned herself so that her back was never to an exit. There were only two places in the world where she felt even a fraction of safety: her home, which she rarely left except for work and the grocery store, and the library itself, where the rows of books created a sense of enclosure she had come to need. Any deviation from these two zones made her heart race. Even a trip to the pharmacy with her husband required hours of mental preparation.

The worst moments came without warning. Sometimes, when she walked past a truck idling at a traffic light, the exhaust would hit her nostrils and she would be back in that truck, her children’s small bodies pressing against her, the men’s voices low and urgent. She would stop in her tracks, unable to move or speak, her vision narrowing until the world reduced to a gray tunnel. She could not describe what happened in those moments to anyone—not to her husband, who had been beside her through all of it and who now watched her with concerned eyes, and not to her doctor, who had asked about her trouble concentrating. That trouble had worsened over the past year. She found herself reading the same page three times, losing the thread of a conversation mid-sentence, forgetting whether she had locked the back door even after checking it twice. At work, she had made two small but noticeable errors in the catalog system, and her supervisor had gently suggested she take a few days off. Maria had refused, because the alternative—sitting at home with nothing to do, without the distraction of busyness—terrified her more than her supervisor’s concern.

It was her husband who finally persuaded her to seek help. He had found her one afternoon in the garage, standing perfectly still, staring at an old cardboard box that contained nothing but their immigration papers and a child’s sweater. She had been crying without making a sound, and when he touched her arm she flinched as though burned. “I can’t keep doing this alone,” he had said, and Maria had nodded because she knew he was right. What she hoped for, sitting across from the therapist, was a way to stop the replaying, the guilt, the smelling of things that were not there. What she feared most was that talking about it would make it real again—that if she said the words out loud, she would break apart completely, and all the busyness and safety and silence she had spent forty years constructing would turn out to be nothing but paper.
